page: Amazon Web Services r8a.48xlarge is a memory-optimized instance built on the Nitro hypervisor architecture. It features 192 dedicated physical cores running on AMD EPYC 9R45 x86_64 processors with a 4.5 GHz clock speed and a 1:1 thread-to-core mapping. Compute resources include 48 KB L1d, 1.0 MB L2, and 32 MB L3 cache, backed by vector instruction sets including AVX-512 with VNNI and BF16 support. Memory provisioning stands at 1536.0 GB of DDR5 operating at 6 GHz, establishing an 8:1 memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU. Network throughput reaches a baseline of 75 Gbps, while no local instance storage or GPUs are bundled.

Benchmark results place the r8a.48xlarge firmly in the top 10% across almost all CPU, memory, and throughput evaluations. It delivers 684882.53 on multi-core stress-ng tests and a multi-core Geekbench score of 27479.0. Memory throughput is significant, posting 1025.61 GB/sec on large-block uncached read operations and 431.72 GB/sec on uncached writes. Database handling capabilities are reinforced by 44395.74 operations in PassMark database testing and 451.09 million operations per second in Redis SET workloads. LLM inference benchmarks demonstrate high prompt-processing efficiency across model sizes, ranging from 5136.48 tokens/sec on 135M parameter models to 55.03 tokens/sec on 70B parameter models.

The qualitative cost profile is aligned with ultra-dense enterprise compute. Consolidating 192 dedicated AMD cores with 1.5 TB of DDR5 memory eliminates the operational complexity of distributed cluster architectures for large datasets. However, the absence of bundled local NVMe storage means external EBS volumes must handle all persistent disk operations, potentially introducing network storage overhead. The absence of GPUs also confines machine learning execution purely to CPU-based inference.

The r8a.48xlarge is suited for memory-intensive enterprise tasks such as distributed in-memory caches, SAP HANA, massive relational databases, large-scale Clang compilation jobs, and real-time big data processing architectures that require high memory bandwidth and vast physical core counts.
